strengths: The paper targets an important practical gap in mathematical-expression recognition: a single system that handles simple typeset, long/complex typeset, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions.

UniMER-1M is potentially valuable in scale and diversity, with 1,061,791 reported training pairs and substantially longer expressions than prior datasets. UniMER-Test also encourages evaluation beyond clean rendered formulas.

The reported results are strong: UniMERNet substantially exceeds Pix2tex and Texify on CPE and SCE, while remaining competitive with specialized handwritten-expression systems across CROHME and HME100K.

The experiments attempt to separate the effects of training-data composition, image augmentation, and the length-aware module, and the qualitative examples illustrate practically meaningful failure modes.
weaknesses: The dataset construction and statistics contain consequential inconsistencies. UniMER-Test is reported as both 23,757 and 23,789 samples; SCE contains either 4,744 or 4,774 samples; and CROHME has either 3,233 or 3,332 test expressions. The stated training-category counts also do not transparently reconcile with the 1,061,791 total. These discrepancies make the benchmark difficult to audit.

Leakage controls are inadequately documented. SPE and CPE are collected from overlapping broad sources such as arXiv, Wikipedia, StackExchange, and Pix2tex, but the paper does not describe source-level splits, near-duplicate detection across train and test, or rendered-image/LaTeX deduplication. Randomly dividing formulas from the same collection pipeline is especially risky for benchmark validity.

The claimed handling of very long expressions is not technically reconciled with the implementation: the dataset reportedly contains sequences up to length 7,037, while the model maximum sequence length is 1,024. The manuscript does not state whether such samples are removed, truncated, or evaluated differently.

The Length-Aware Module is underspecified and only weakly supported as the principal methodological novelty. It is alternately described as predicting overall sequence length and mapping features into symbol-category space, without defining its target representation, dimensionality, inference behavior, or precise decoder conditioning. Its ablation improves CPE BLEU from 0.893 to 0.916 but is neutral or slightly harmful on several other metric/subset combinations, with no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates.

Several reported numbers and conclusions are erroneous. In Table 3, the Pix2tex/no-augmentation HWE edit distance is 0.004 despite BLEU 0.087 and conflicts with the corresponding 0.775 elsewhere. UniMERNet does not surpass every HME100K result as claimed: its 68.0 ExpRate and 89.6 within-two rate are below CAN-ABM's 68.1 and 89.9. Some stated improvement margins also do not match the tables.

The comparison evidence is too narrow for the broad universal/SOTA claims. Only Pix2tex and Texify receive quantitative evaluation on the unified benchmark; Nougat appears only in three adapted qualitative examples, and Vary is not evaluated. Model size, pretraining, training data, and decoding conditions are not controlled or reported, limiting fairness.

Evaluation preprocessing is not specified. LaTeX permits many semantically equivalent strings, so BLEU, edit distance, and exact match depend strongly on tokenization and normalization. The paper does not explain these procedures, nor does it report performance by expression length to directly validate the length-aware claim.

Reproducibility is presently poor: the abstract's release URL is blank, and essential details such as dataset manifests and licenses, precise train/test composition, tokenizer, image resizing, augmentation probabilities and strengths, architecture sizes, decoding settings, and inference cost are missing. The implementation section also contradicts itself by first describing single-GPU training and then four-GPU training.

Overall, the scale and reported performance are promising, but unresolved benchmark integrity, inconsistent results, and insufficient specification materially weaken the central empirical claims; these are more than presentation-only issues.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/2a1e039ee55344629aaf37f7fe03c62f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important practical problem: recognizing mathematical expressions across printed, screen-captured, and handwritten inputs rather than optimizing for a single domain.

UniMER-1M is potentially valuable because it substantially expands the scale and length diversity of MER training data. UniMER-Test also attempts a useful four-way decomposition into simple printed, complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions.

The reported aggregate performance is strong. UniMERNet substantially exceeds Pix2tex and Texify on the proposed CPE and SCE subsets and is competitive with specialized handwritten-recognition systems across several CROHME benchmarks.

The authors provide ablations for training-data composition, augmentation, and the Length-Aware Module. In particular, augmentation gives a meaningful reported gain on SCE when training on UniMER-1M, from 0.559 to 0.616 BLEU.
weaknesses: The principal model contribution is not convincingly supported. In Table 4, LAM clearly helps only CPE: it improves BLEU from 0.893 to 0.916 and edit distance from 0.065 to 0.060. It slightly worsens both SPE metrics, worsens SCE edit distance from 0.227 to 0.229, and is essentially neutral on HWE. No repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, length-prediction accuracy, or performance-versus-length analysis substantiate the broad claim that LAM significantly improves recognition across varying complexities.

The state-of-the-art comparison confounds method quality with training data. UniMERNet is trained on over one million mixed-domain examples, while Pix2tex and Texify appear to be evaluated as existing pretrained models rather than retrained on UniMER-1M under matched conditions. The ablations themselves show that changing the training corpus produces much larger gains than adding LAM. Consequently, Tables 5–6 support the value of the combined data-and-model system but do not establish architectural superiority.

Dataset accounting contains multiple unresolved contradictions: Table 1 reports 23,757 test samples while the subset counts sum to 23,789; the SCE set is reported as both 4,774 and 4,744 samples; and the CROHME test count appears as both 3,233 and 3,332. The construction description also does not provide a complete split accounting or explain cross-source and cross-split deduplication. Because mined LaTeX sources can overlap with existing rendered datasets, the absence of contamination checks is consequential.

The long-expression claim is inadequately evaluated. The dataset reportedly contains strings up to length 7,037, but the model has a maximum sequence length of 1,024. The paper neither explains truncation or filtering nor reports what fraction of examples exceeds the model limit. Aggregate CPE scores cannot demonstrate robustness across the claimed length range.

Several reported details undermine confidence in correctness. Table 3 lists HWE edit distance as 0.004 without augmentation and 0.775 with augmentation for Pix2tex training, contradicting both the corresponding BLEU values and the assertion of consistent augmentation improvements. The implementation section also says training uses a single GPU and then specifies four A100 GPUs.

The method is insufficiently specified for reproduction. LAM alternates between descriptions as a scalar length predictor, a symbol-category counting vector, and a length embedding; its exact targets and tensor transformations are unclear. Tokenization, vocabulary, input resizing, encoder/decoder configurations, decoding procedure, augmentation probabilities and magnitudes, normalization used for string metrics, checkpoints, and random seeds are not provided.

The evaluation does not adequately validate the claimed universal, real-world applicability. SCE is drawn from cropped formulas in 1,000 PDF pages, while photographs and other stated acquisition conditions are not separately tested. BLEU and character edit distance also fail to account for visually or semantically equivalent LaTeX, and the paper reports neither rendering-based equivalence nor syntax/compilation validity.

The dataset is potentially the strongest contribution, but its documentation is not publication-ready: sampling rules, source proportions, annotation agreement or error rates, licensing and redistribution status, and a usable resource link are absent from the submitted manuscript. Overall, the promising scale and results do not outweigh the fairness, validation, dataset-integrity, and reproducibility concerns in the current evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical gap in mathematical-expression recognition by jointly covering simple printed, complex/long, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions, rather than optimizing for only one setting.

UniMER is a potentially valuable resource: UniMER-1M is substantially larger and more diverse than the cited alternatives, while UniMER-Test contains roughly 23.8K examples and includes a manually annotated, cross-verified screen-capture subset.

The empirical gains are strong. On UniMER-Test, UniMERNet reaches BLEU scores of 0.916 on CPE, 0.616 on SCE, and 0.921 on HWE, substantially exceeding Pix2tex and Texify. It also obtains competitive or best reported exact-match results across the evaluated CROHME benchmarks.

The ablations provide useful evidence that the expanded training data and image augmentation drive meaningful improvements, especially on complex, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions. The length-aware module gives a focused improvement on CPE without substantially changing the other subsets.

The problem formulation, dataset categories, overall architecture, and principal experimental findings are presented clearly, and the proposed system has credible practical utility for scientific-document processing.
weaknesses: The comparison is not sufficiently controlled to attribute gains to the architecture: UniMERNet benefits from over one million diverse training instances, while Pix2tex and Texify are evaluated in their existing forms. Competitor architectures retrained on UniMER-1M would better separate the effects of data, augmentation, and model design. The printed-expression comparison also includes only two specialized baselines and is dated for a CVPR 2026 submission.

The evidence for the length-aware module is modest. It improves CPE BLEU from 0.893 to 0.916, but slightly worsens both SPE metrics and SCE edit distance. No length-stratified analysis, length-prediction accuracy, statistical variability, or comparison to simpler length-control mechanisms is provided, making the broad claims about varied-length recognition stronger than the evidence.

Dataset accounting contains consequential inconsistencies: UniMER-Test is reported as 23,757 in Table 1 but its listed subsets sum to 23,789; SCE is variously reported as 4,774 and 4,744; and the stated training-source counts do not transparently reconcile with the claimed 1,061,791 total. The train/test deduplication procedure, especially for formulas collected from overlapping web sources, is also insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript ends the availability statement without a link and omits model size, image preprocessing/resolution policy, tokenizer and normalization details, augmentation probabilities, decoding procedure, and sufficiently precise dataset split construction. Table 3 additionally reports an implausible HWE edit distance of 0.004 for the non-augmented Pix2tex setting, inconsistent with its BLEU of 0.087 and with the surrounding results.

The model uses a maximum output length of 1,024 while the dataset reports expressions as long as 7,037 characters, yet the paper gives no truncation rate or performance beyond this limit. This qualifies the claim of handling highly complex and long expressions. There is also no evaluation of inference cost, robustness across distinct real-world sources, or rendered/structural equivalence beyond string-based metrics.

strengths: The central dataset contribution is potentially valuable: UniMER combines printed, long/complex, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions, while the 4,744 manually corrected screen-captured examples address conditions poorly represented by conventional rendered-formula benchmarks.

The controlled comparison against Texify trained on the same UniMER-1M data is informative. UniMERNet-B improves BLEU from 0.906/0.900/0.599/0.888 to 0.915/0.925/0.626/0.895 on SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE, and the smaller variants expose useful accuracy-throughput tradeoffs.

The paper includes component, augmentation, pretraining, and depth ablations. In particular, the architecture ablation indicates that most accuracy improvement comes from FGE and convolutional enhancement, while squeeze attention raises reported throughput from 4.07 to 5.04 images/s with only small accuracy changes.
The motivation is practically relevant, and the manuscript is generally readable, with clear diagrams, dataset examples, and compact quantitative tables.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction is not documented sufficiently to establish split integrity. Training formulas and the 16-million-pair pretraining corpus are largely extracted from arXiv, while the SCE test set includes unspecified papers and other documents. Only within-SCE perceptual-hash deduplication is described; there is no source-, expression-, or image-level leakage check between training/pretraining and any test subset. This is consequential because the main gains, especially on CPE and SCE, could be affected by overlap.

Dataset accounting is internally inconsistent and incomplete. UniMER-Test is reported as both 23,789 and 23,757 samples; the text does not give the SPE/CPE test counts; and the stated component sizes do not transparently reconcile with the reported 1,061,791 training samples. The description that 110,332 CPE formulas are selected 'for training and test sets' provides no split. These issues prevent independent reconstruction and weaken confidence in the evaluation.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted manuscript. The promised code/data URL and dataset footnote are blank, the normalization rules are only described at a high level, and the influential 16-million-pair 'in-house' pretraining set lacks a releasable specification. Key training details such as image preprocessing/resolution, augmentation probabilities, optimizer, tokenizer/vocabulary, decoding procedure, and random seeds are missing.

Squeeze Attention, the main decoder novelty, is specified only as projecting queries and keys to a lower-dimensional space. The projection dimensions, exact equations, affected attention layers, computational complexity, and implementation details are absent. Consequently, neither the technical behavior nor the claimed speedup can be independently verified from the paper.

The evidence does not fully support the broad state-of-the-art and robustness claims. Comparisons cover only a few systems, strong handwritten-MER methods discussed in related work are not evaluated, and ExpRate is defined but never reported. Original baselines use different training data, while the fair Texify* comparison shows materially smaller architecture gains than comparisons emphasized against original Texify. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are provided for these relatively small gains.

The evaluation protocol is underspecified: BLEU tokenization and EditDis normalization are not defined, despite LaTeX admitting many equivalent strings. There is no rendering-based or semantic-equivalence metric and no annotation-quality audit for SCE. Throughput is reported only for batch size 128 with a maximum sequence length of 1536, without actual length distributions, latency, memory, decoding settings, or complete hardware/software details, limiting the practical speed claim.

Several numerical and experimental inconsistencies further reduce confidence: model parameter counts differ across tables (e.g., UniMERNet-T is 100M versus 107M, and the stated Texify-like baseline is 342M versus 312M), and pretrained Texify has CPE BLEU 0.900 in Table 5 but 0.903 in Table 6. These are correctable presentation issues individually, but alongside the split and protocol omissions they make the reported comparisons difficult to audit.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important vision problem that is underrepresented by clean rendered-expression benchmarks: recognizing long, noisy, screen-captured, and handwritten mathematical expressions.

UniMER-1M is potentially valuable because it combines more than one million examples, length-aware sampling, multiple rendering fonts and resolutions, handwritten data, and extensive image degradation augmentations.

The experiments provide useful controlled comparisons. In particular, retraining Texify on UniMER-1M (Texify*) substantially improves its CPE, SCE, and HWE results, providing credible evidence that the expanded training data is beneficial independently of the proposed architecture.

The architecture ablation, augmentation study, model-size variants, and encoder/decoder depth studies expose meaningful accuracy-throughput tradeoffs. The final architectural changes improve throughput from 4.12 to 5.06 images/s while producing modest accuracy improvements over the stated baseline.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction is insufficiently specified to establish a fair evaluation. CPE training and test examples are sampled from the same large collection, but the split unit is not stated and no cross-split exact or near-duplicate analysis is reported. Document-level separation is especially important because formulas from the same papers can recur or share highly similar notation. Only SCE receives a described deduplication procedure, and that procedure is apparently internal to SCE rather than across training, pretraining, and test data.

The main results have an unresolved pretraining confound. Table 6 shows that the reported UniMERNet-B scores of 0.915/0.925/0.626/0.895 use an additional in-house collection of 16 million ArXiv-derived image-text pairs. The same scores are presented elsewhere as results of training with UniMER-1M, while the implementation and ablation sections also state that models are trained from scratch. It is therefore unclear which results use the unavailable pretraining data or whether its source documents overlap UniMER-Test. This materially weakens both the empirical attribution and reproducibility.

The evaluation is too narrow for the claims of a universal model and a new benchmark. Quantitative comparison is largely limited to Pix2tex and Texify; modern dedicated handwritten-MER methods cited in the paper are not evaluated. Nougat appears only in three adapted qualitative examples. ExpRate is defined but never reported, and no rendering-based or semantic-equivalence metric is used despite the acknowledged ambiguity of LaTeX strings.

Several dataset statistics conflict. UniMER-Test is reported as containing both 23,789 and 23,757 samples; the CROHME test count is given as both 3,332 and 3,233; the stated component counts do not transparently reconcile with the 1,061,791-example training total; and the CPE train/test allocation is not provided. These are basic benchmark-integrity issues rather than cosmetic presentation errors.

The new architecture is only incrementally original, combining an overlapping convolutional stem, depthwise convolutional enhancement, removal of shifted windows, and lower-dimensional attention. More importantly, essential specifications are absent: the squeeze dimension and exact attention computation are not given, the placement and repetition of ConvEnhance are ambiguous, and the architecture is not defined precisely enough to reproduce from the manuscript.

Metric and experimental details are incomplete. BLEU tokenization, n-gram order, smoothing, and aggregation are unspecified; EditDis appears normalized but its normalization is not defined; there are no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates; and the FPS comparison omits important decoding and input-shape details. Parameter counts also disagree between Tables 4 and 5 for UniMERNet-T (100M versus 107M).

The real-world and comprehensiveness claims are overstated. Two evaluation subsets are rendered, HWE reuses existing datasets, and the only newly collected real-world subset contains 4,744 screen-captured crops from 1,000 pages. There is no evaluation on photographs, severe perspective variation, or broader acquisition domains, nor an annotation-agreement or label-quality audit for SCE.

Reproducibility is currently poor: the manuscript ends the availability statement with no usable URL, relies on an in-house 16-million-pair pretraining corpus, does not provide exact splits, and gives contradictory hardware wording ('a single GPU' followed by eight A100 GPUs). Overall, the dataset direction and same-data Texify comparison are worthwhile, but the benchmark-integrity and pretraining-attribution problems prevent the evidence from supporting the paper's broad claims, so the balance favors weak rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important gap in mathematical-expression recognition by covering simple printed, complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions rather than focusing only on clean rendered formulas.

The dataset contribution is substantial: UniMER-1M contains over one million image-LaTeX pairs, while UniMER-Test explicitly targets complexity and real-world appearance. The documented variation in formula length, fonts, DPI, and image augmentation is useful for robustness research.

The experiments separate the benefits of training data from those of architecture. Under matched UniMER-1M training, UniMERNet-B improves over Texify* from 0.900 to 0.925 BLEU on CPE and from 0.599 to 0.626 on SCE, while also increasing throughput from 4.16 to 5.06 images/s.

The architectural ablations are informative: fine-grained embedding and convolutional enhancement improve recognition, while squeeze attention and removal of shifted windows reduce parameters and yield roughly a 23% throughput improvement with little accuracy loss. Multiple model sizes also expose useful accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs.

The appendix provides valuable additional evidence on data augmentation, pretraining, encoder/decoder depth, rendering settings, normalization, and dataset distributions. Overall, the supported dataset and efficiency contributions are useful even though the architectural novelty is incremental.
weaknesses: The benchmark accounting is internally inconsistent and needs resolution. The text reports 23,789 UniMER-Test samples, Table 1 reports 23,757, yet the stated Pix2tex test set used as SPE alone contains 30,637 samples. The CPE train/test split sizes are also not reported separately. These discrepancies materially weaken confidence in the benchmark definition.

Potential leakage and near-duplicate contamination are insufficiently addressed. Printed training and test formulas are drawn from overlapping source domains such as arXiv, Wikipedia, and StackExchange, but no document-level split or cross-split textual/image deduplication is described. Perceptual-hash deduplication is discussed only within SCE.

The comparison breadth is narrower than claims such as outperforming all previous methods suggest. Numerical evaluation includes mainly Pix2tex and Texify; strong specialized handwritten-MER systems are not evaluated, Nougat appears only qualitatively, and ExpRate is defined as a standard metric but never reported.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Squeeze Attention lacks its projection dimensions and a precise mathematical specification; augmentation probabilities and several preprocessing/sampling details are omitted. The main results also use 16 million in-house image-text pretraining pairs whose exact construction, split hygiene, and availability are unclear.

Most of the accuracy improvement comes from the new data rather than the network design. Relative to the same-data Texify* baseline, architectural gains are modest on SPE and HWE, and UniMERNet-T is worse on SCE. The paper should frame the model contribution more conservatively.

The evaluation reports single runs without uncertainty, and token-level BLEU/edit distance may penalize visually equivalent LaTeX despite normalization. Exact-match or rendering-based results would better substantiate practical recognition quality. These limitations are meaningful but do not outweigh the demonstrated dataset and efficiency contribution.
